---
title: "How it works"
subtitle: "Statistics first, then a bounded agent loop, then a gate that deletes claims it cannot verify."
---

## The whole pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  BUNDLE[Incident recording in Parquet] --> SCORE[Score every service]
  SCORE --> RANK[Walk the call graph]
  RANK --> GATE1{Unusual enough?}
  GATE1 -->|No| OUT2[Abstain, naming the threshold]
  GATE1 -->|Yes| LOOP[Agent loop]
  LOOP --> GATE2[Six verification checks]
  GATE2 -->|Claims survive| OUT1[Report with citations]
  GATE2 -->|Support too thin| OUT2
```

The first three boxes use no model at all.

## Why statistics run first

Two reasons.

**Cost.** Reading forty services to find one costs forty times the tokens of reading three.

**A baseline you can compare against.** The statistics step alone is a configuration called
`b0`. Every agent configuration has to beat it. A multi-agent system that cannot beat a page of
statistics should not exist, and that comparison is reported either way.

### Median instead of mean

A fault is a spike. A spike pulls the mean towards itself and inflates the standard deviation,
so scoring the spike against statistics that include it makes the spike look smaller than it is.

Firebreak uses the median and the median absolute deviation instead. A spike barely moves
either, so it stays visible.

## Why the call graph matters

When payment breaks, the frontend's error rate rises too, because every request passes through
it. The frontend looks worse and is not the cause.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  USER[Requests] --> FRONTEND[frontend]
  FRONTEND --> CHECKOUT[checkout]
  CHECKOUT --> PAYMENT[payment is broken]
  FRONTEND --> OTHER[other services are fine]
```

Firebreak walks this graph from the services that look unusual and asks which single service best
explains the whole pattern.

::: {.callout-important}
## On real recordings this does not work yet

On the eight recordings available, the ranking blames `frontend` for all three payment failures.
That is the symptom winning over the cause, which is the exact thing this step exists to prevent.

It is the second largest open problem in the project, and it is recorded with its evidence rather
than smoothed over.
:::

## The four roles

What each one cannot do matters more than what it does.

| Role | Does | Cannot | Why the limit exists |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commander | Picks the next theory and who tests it | Call an evidence tool | Separates deciding what to look at from looking |
| Specialists | Gather evidence, one question each | See each other's answers | Four independent looks, not a conversation converging on the first guess |
| Critic | Argues against the leading theory | Gather new evidence | It can only test the case on the table, not build its own |
| Reporter | Writes claims naming their evidence | Cite a record no tool produced | The gate re-runs every citation, so an invented one fails |

## How a tool call works

A model never writes a query. It chooses a tool and supplies arguments; the tool builds the
query.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  PICK[Model picks a tool] --> VALID[Arguments validated]
  VALID --> BUILD[Tool builds the query]
  BUILD --> DB[(Backend)]
  DB --> CAP[Row cap applied]
  CAP --> REC[Evidence record saved]
```

The evidence record holds the query, the time window, a fingerprint of the backend, a hash of the
rows, and the arguments needed to run it again. Its identifier is a hash of what was asked and
what came back.

That buys three things:

1. **A query nobody can inject into.** The realistic attack here is a log line, not a prompt.
2. **A cap on every call**, so one tool cannot fill the context window.
3. **An identifier that makes re-execution meaningful**, which is what the gate depends on.

## The six checks

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  CLAIM[A claim] --> IDS[Its evidence ids]
  IDS --> RERUN[Re-run each query]
  RERUN --> SAME{Same row hash?}
  SAME -->|Yes| KEEP[Claim kept]
  SAME -->|No| DROP[Claim deleted]
```

| Check | Rejects |
|---|---|
| `coverage` | A claim citing an id nothing recorded |
| `re_execution` | A citation that no longer returns the same rows |
| `numbers` | A number in prose that its evidence does not contain |
| `consistency` | A report that disagrees with the investigation log |
| `confidence_sanity` | Confidence the evidence does not support |
| `abstention` | Naming a service whose support is below the threshold |

::: {.callout-warning}
## What the gate cannot check

Whether a claim says anything useful.

All 40 claims across the ten demo reports are true, cited, re-runnable and uninformative. Four
of every five describe the investigation rather than the incident, because they come from a
deterministic stub rather than a model.

Six checks ask whether a claim is *supported*. None asks whether it is *informative*. Whether to
add a seventh is an open question, not a quiet change.
:::

## Keeping the answer away from the agent

A benchmark is worthless if the system under test can read the answer. This is made impossible
rather than discouraged.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  LABELS[(Ground truth labels)] --> EVAL[Evaluation code only]
  LABELS -. import blocked .-> AGENT[Agent packages]
  CANARY[Canary string in every label] --> SCAN[Every prompt scanned]
  FLAGS[Fault flag changes] -. removed .-> LOG[Change log the agent reads]
```

Four controls carry most of the weight:

1. Labels live in a separate package that only the evaluation code may import, enforced by a test
   that walks the import graph rather than searching text, so an alias cannot hide.
2. Every label contains a random canary string, and every prompt sent to a model is scanned for
   it.
3. The change log the agent reads has fault flag changes removed, or the answer would be sitting
   in the evidence.
4. Memory may only be written for training scenarios, because "payment failed like this last
   time" is the answer wearing a different hat.

That import test has caught two real paths during development. Neither was a leak; both were
routes a leak could later have travelled.
